Introduction

The electric vehicle revolution is accelerating faster than ever before. As EV adoption continues to surge across the United States, one critical challenge looms: ensuring robust, reliable, and accessible charging infrastructure to support this growth. In 2025, the EV charging landscape is experiencing unprecedented expansion, with new technologies, innovative business models, and significant government investments reshaping how Americans charge their vehicles. At Shaffer Construction, Inc., we're at the forefront of this transformation, helping Los Angeles property owners and businesses build the charging infrastructure they need for the electric future. Whether you're planning residential EV charger installation or commercial charging networks, understanding the trends and challenges is essential to making informed decisions about your investment and long-term electrical needs.

Record Growth: America's EV Charging Boom in 2025

The United States is experiencing a charging infrastructure boom unprecedented in scale. According to recent industry data, America is on track to add 16,700 new fast-charging ports by the end of 2025—approximately 2.4 times the number deployed in 2022. This represents a remarkable 20% year-over-year increase that demonstrates how seriously the nation is taking EV infrastructure development at every level of government and in the private sector.

The statistics are staggering. In 2024 alone, more than 40,000 new non-home chargers were deployed across the country, surpassing any previous year. As reported by the International Energy Agency's 2025 Global EV Outlook, public EV charging points have grown exponentially over the past decade, from approximately 30,000 in 2016 to nearly 196,000 in January 2025. This six-fold increase reflects sustained commitment at federal, state, and local levels to build the infrastructure necessary for mass EV adoption. The growth trajectory suggests that within just a few years, finding a charging station will be as ubiquitous as finding a gas station.

California, and specifically Los Angeles, leads the nation in this transformation. California now has at least three times more EV chargers than any other state, a testament to the region's environmental commitment and the high concentration of EV owners. The infrastructure boom is not just about quantity—it's about accessibility, reliability, and strategic placement that serves both urban centers and rural areas. Shaffer Construction understands that building this infrastructure requires expertise in electrical systems, permitting, and long-term reliability planning. Our team has worked on numerous charging installations and understands the unique challenges of Los Angeles infrastructure.

The Shift to Ultra-Fast Charging Technology

One of the most significant trends in 2025 is the dramatic shift toward high-power charging solutions. The share of ultra-fast 250+ kW chargers has jumped from 25% to 38% of all new installations, while traditional 24-149 kW units have declined from 33% to 28%. This transition reflects the industry's response to consumer demand for faster charging times and improved convenience, as drivers increasingly expect charging speeds comparable to refueling at a gasoline station.

Major charging operators are now deploying 350 kW and 400 kW chargers as standard, a significant upgrade from the speeds available just a few years ago. These megawatt-level charging stations paired with battery storage systems represent the future of fast charging, though they require sophisticated electrical infrastructure to support them. For property owners in Los Angeles considering commercial EV charger installation, this evolution means that modern solutions can provide significantly faster charging experiences for customers and employees. A 350 kW charger can add 200 miles of range in just 15-20 minutes, dramatically improving the user experience.

The trend toward larger, higher-powered charging stations is also changing the user experience. Non-Tesla charging stations now average 3.8 ports per location, while Tesla Superchargers average 15.1 ports, reducing wait times and improving reliability across the network. This consolidation of charging power into fewer, larger hubs is shaping how Los Angeles and surrounding regions plan their charging networks. Instead of scattering single chargers across neighborhoods, the industry is moving toward regional charging hubs that serve larger areas more efficiently.

As discussed in our guide to emerging trends in EV charger installation, understanding these technological advances is crucial for making informed decisions about your property's charging needs. The infrastructure you install today should be capable of supporting faster charging speeds in the future, even if you don't immediately deploy ultra-fast charging equipment.

Los Angeles: Leading California's EV Charging Revolution

Los Angeles is experiencing unprecedented growth in EV infrastructure development, positioning itself as a national leader in the transition to zero-emission transportation. In November 2025, the City of Los Angeles Department of Transportation announced an ambitious plan to deploy 90 new curbside Level-2 charging ports across the city over the next 12 months. These chargers, available 24/7 at convenient curbside locations, represent the city's commitment to making charging accessible to residents and visitors alike, particularly those without private parking.

Beyond street-level charging, Los Angeles County has adopted its first-ever Zero-Emission Vehicle Master Plan, which sets aggressive goals for EV infrastructure expansion. The County aims to install 15,000 EV chargers on public properties by 2035, with over 750 chargers already operating at County facilities. Los Angeles County also oversees projects like the PowerFlex initiative in Long Beach, which recently installed 20 new Level 2 charging ports in the Carmelitos community, demonstrating the commitment to equitable infrastructure deployment across diverse neighborhoods.

The Mayor's Sustainable pLAn amplifies these efforts with a goal of increasing EV adoption by 25%, adding 100,000 new electric vehicles in the City by 2025. This aggressive target reflects Los Angeles' recognition that charging infrastructure is essential for meeting climate goals and reducing harmful emissions that impact public health. Shaffer Construction is actively participating in this transformation, helping businesses and property owners build the charging solutions necessary to support this growth. Our residential EV charger installation services ensure that Los Angeles homeowners can charge efficiently and safely at home, while our commercial solutions support the public and private charging networks expanding across the region. We understand the specific electrical codes and permitting requirements unique to Los Angeles and Los Angeles County.

Challenges and Solutions in EV Infrastructure Development

Despite the rapid growth, significant challenges remain that require creative solutions and careful planning. According to the Paren Q2 2025 State of the Industry Report, grid infrastructure constraints pose a major limitation to charging deployment. Ultra-high-power chargers require substantial electrical upgrades, and many areas face limitations in grid capacity that could slow deployment. This is particularly relevant in Los Angeles, where aging electrical infrastructure in some neighborhoods requires careful planning and engineering to support new charging infrastructure. Some areas may need complete electrical panel upgrades or new service lines to accommodate fast charging.

Profitability remains another challenge facing charging operators. Many charging companies report negative EBITDA margins as they prioritize network expansion over short-term profits, investing heavily in infrastructure before revenue reaches sustainable levels. However, this competitive pressure is benefiting consumers through improved reliability and faster charging speeds. For property owners considering EV infrastructure investments, understanding these market dynamics helps inform financial projections and timing decisions. The cost of installing charging infrastructure is declining as economies of scale develop and competition intensifies.

Standardization issues also persist, though they are being resolved. Different regions use different connector types—CHAdeMO, CCS1, CCS2, and GB/T—creating interoperability challenges and requiring multiple connector types. Most new installations in the United States are standardizing on CCS1 and Tesla's North American Charging Standard (NACS), which simplifies decisions for new projects. This standardization will make it easier for drivers to use any charging network regardless of their vehicle type.

The regulatory landscape continues to evolve to support infrastructure development. Government funding through programs like NEVI (National Electric Vehicle Infrastructure) provides crucial support for corridor charging, while community-focused grants fund local network development. As of early 2025, the Department of Transportation announced $635 million in grants to continue building EV charging infrastructure, with $368 million allocated for community projects and $268 million for corridor fast-charging projects. These funds help offset the massive upfront costs of infrastructure deployment.

Planning Your EV Infrastructure: What Property Owners Should Know

For Los Angeles property owners and businesses considering EV charging infrastructure, success requires careful planning and professional execution. As outlined in our comprehensive guide to planning EV charger infrastructure installation in Los Angeles, the process involves electrical assessment, permitting, installation, and ongoing maintenance. The decisions made during the planning phase will impact the performance, cost, and long-term viability of your charging infrastructure.

The first step is understanding your property's electrical capacity. Residential installations typically require 240-volt circuits and may necessitate panel upgrades, while commercial properties need more complex load calculations. The relationship between your existing electrical infrastructure and your charging goals is critical—this is where electrical expertise becomes invaluable. Shaffer Construction conducts thorough electrical assessments to determine what upgrades are necessary, ensuring your charging installation is safe, efficient, and compliant with all local codes. We help property owners understand their options, from simple Level 1 chargers to advanced Level 3 DC fast charging stations.

Los Angeles building codes and electrical standards continue to evolve to accommodate EV charging infrastructure. Building permits, electrical inspections, and utility coordination are essential steps that should never be skipped. Our team at Shaffer Construction handles all permitting requirements, managing relationships with the City of Los Angeles Department of Building and Safety and local utility providers. We ensure that every installation meets current code requirements and passes all required inspections.

The future of EV charging is not just about the equipment—it's about integration with the broader electrical grid, potential smart charging capabilities, and future scalability. Modern charging installations should be designed with future expansion in mind, allowing property owners to add additional charging ports as their needs grow. Installing conduit and electrical infrastructure for future charging ports during initial installation is far more cost-effective than retrofitting later.

The Future Outlook: What's Next for EV Charging

Looking ahead, projections indicate explosive growth in EV charging infrastructure across the United States. If current trends continue, the United States will have 100,000 public fast-charging ports by 2027, more than double the current number. Looking further forward to 2030, the number of charge points in the U.S. is forecast to rise from approximately 4 million currently to 35 million. This represents an eight-fold increase in just five years, demonstrating the massive investment and effort being directed toward charging infrastructure.

Emerging companies like Ionna, Mercedes-Benz High Power Charging, BP Pulse, and Walmart are entering the market, creating new competition and driving innovation. This "Charging 2.0" phase emphasizes quality, reliability, and user experience over pure network expansion. For property owners, this means more options, better technology, and increased support for making informed infrastructure decisions. Competition is driving down costs while improving service quality and uptime.

Energy storage integration represents another frontier in EV charging infrastructure. Pairing high-power chargers with battery storage systems helps alleviate peak grid demand and optimizes energy usage. This technology is particularly relevant for California, which frequently experiences peak demand periods during summer months. Battery storage allows charging stations to operate without exceeding local grid capacity, solving one of the major infrastructure constraints preventing faster deployment.

Conclusion

The rise of EV charging infrastructure in 2025 represents one of the most significant transformations in transportation and energy infrastructure in a generation. From record deployment numbers to technological advances in ultra-fast charging, from Los Angeles' aggressive local goals to federal funding initiatives, the momentum is clear: America is building the charging infrastructure needed to support mass EV adoption. The question is no longer whether charging infrastructure will exist, but rather how quickly it will be deployed and how well it will be integrated with the electrical grid.

For Los Angeles property owners and businesses, this transformation presents both opportunity and responsibility. Building the right charging infrastructure today ensures you're prepared for the electric future while potentially increasing property value and customer satisfaction. The decisions you make now—about capacity, technology, and placement—will impact your property for years to come. Early adopters often benefit from lower costs and availability of premium locations.
